scope.flow: packedFloat comparison functions (eq, lt) operating on raw representation instead of mathematical value
scope.environment: Solidity library with packedFloat alias for uint256; dependent lending protocol using Float128.lt for liquidation checks

entities.name: lending protocol user whose position is liquidated
dependent lending protocol performing liquidation check

statements.text: pfThreshold has mathematical value 10 and is stored in normalized form (mantissa 1e37, exponent -36).
pfCollateral has mathematical value 1000 but is provided in a non-normalized representation (mantissa 1e40, exponent -37) that the protocol wraps directly.
The collateral's mathematical value 1000 is greater than the liquidation threshold 10, so no liquidation should occur.
The protocol performs the check Float128.lt(pfCollateral, pfThreshold) to decide whether to liquidate.
The lt function compares raw exponents/mantissas directly without normalizing, so with matching signs it compares pfCollateral's exponent -37 against pfThreshold's -36.
Since -37 < -36, lt incorrectly returns true for mathematically equal-or-greater collateral.
Liquidation is wrongfully triggered even though the collateral's mathematical value 1000 was much greater than the threshold 10.
Comparisons between mathematically equal but differently represented numbers fail, violating fundamental mathematical expectations and enabling critical logic failures in dependent contracts.
Comparison functions should compare the mathematical value of packedFloat inputs, so that mathematically equal values compare equal and a value above a threshold is not reported as below it.
A position whose collateral mathematical value is above the liquidation threshold should not be liquidated.

ambiguities: Report does not state whether the attacker is an unauthorized caller or has any specific permission; oracle influence is described only as a scenario assumption.
The lending protocol and oracle are hypothetical examples, not observed deployments.
Whether the protocol actually wraps the oracle value directly without normalization is assumed, not established.
No concrete loss amount or affected user count is reported beyond the single example.
